e1:
“Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become compulsory disclosure, where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. A group starts out inviting honesty and ends up treating privacy as resistance.

Peer counseling can become peer surveillance, even if the tone is warm. And when there are pre-reqs for people to get medicine, they can put power in the hands of gatekeepers, right when people are at their most open. Even something couched in words like “willing to be seen” could become a demand that people disclose whatever the group wants them to.

The boundary is simple. These principles aren't things that give the community power over me, they're commitments I choose for my own practice.
e2:
“Nothing suppressed” applies to myself and my relationship with my own material. It doesn't give anyone the right to pull anything out of me. Any member can choose not to share material, and they don't need to provide a therapeutic rationale for not sharing.

The medicine is optional. Choosing not to take the medicine in no way affects anyone's rights as a member. The power to let people into the group doesn't sit with any individual or permanent clique. And disagreement has to be answered as disagreement.

“Your resistance is your wound talking” is pretty much a conversation ender. Once you notice a community diagnosing dissent like this instead of answering it, leave before they schedule a group process about your leaving.

There are some basics that the majority cannot vote away from any member of a community. These basics are your bodily safety, adequate food and sleep, the right to go to a doctor of your choice, the right to keep your thoughts private, the right to communicate with people outside the community, a way to report harm without asking the accused person's friends for permission, and a usable way to leave. Removing these from a community member is not consensual, even if a majority vote does it.
